Model selection: the evidence for the number of classes

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/model-selection.Rmd
model-selection.Rmd

A mixture model does not estimate its own number of classes. The analyst fits a range of candidates and chooses among them, and that choice is argued from evidence rather than computed. latents reports the evidence in full and selects nothing. This guide describes every piece of that evidence: what each table and plot computes, how it is read, where it misleads, and how the pieces are combined into a choice that can be stated and defended. The worked example in Class enumeration in mixture models applies the same tools to one analysis from start to finish; this guide is the reference behind it.

The evidence falls into five kinds, each answering a different question.

Question Evidence Verbs
Which candidate balances fit and size best? Information criteria and their minima as.data.frame(), get_results(x, "best"), plot(x)
Where do added classes stop paying off? Changes between neighbouring candidates and the knee of each curve get_results(x, "deltas"), get_results(x, "knees"), plot(x, what = "deltas"), plot(x, what = "heatmap")
Are the classes distinct? Entropy, average posterior probability, odds of correct classification get_results(x, "classification"), plot(x, what = "diagnostics")
Can the estimate be trusted? Convergence, boundary estimates, replication of the best likelihood, the smallest class plot(x, what = "trust"), plot(x, what = "smallest")
Is one more class supported? The bootstrap likelihood ratio test of neighbouring candidates bootstrap_lrt()

plot(x, what = "selection") draws the plots of the second, third and fourth rows together, and compare_models() places chosen candidates side by side.

library(latents)

The candidates

The examples use course_engagement: course enrolments nested in students, with five standardized measures of activity per enrolment. Every combination of one to six profiles and one to four group classes is fitted with a covariance structure of free variances and zero covariances ("VVI"). Three random starts per candidate keep the example short; applied analyses use ten or more, because replication of the best likelihood across starts is itself part of the evidence.

activity <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
models

The grid holds 24 candidates, of which 21 were fitted. A candidate with one profile and several group classes is not identified, because group classes that share a single profile cannot differ, so it is listed and left unfitted. Every candidate is named by its numbers of classes, profiles4_groups3 for four profiles and three group classes, and the verbs below accept that name.

Information criteria

Definitions

Each criterion starts from the deviance, -2L, where L is the maximized log likelihood, and adds a charge. With q free parameters, n the sample size and EN the classification entropy, EN = -sum(p log p) summed over every unit and class of the posterior probabilities p:

Criterion Formula Charge depends on Reference
aic -2L + 2q parameters only Akaike (1974)
kic -2L + 3(q + 1) parameters only Cavanaugh (1999)
bic -2L + q log(n) sample size Schwarz (1978)
sabic -2L + q log((n + 2) / 24) sample size Sclove (1987)
caic -2L + q (log(n) + 1) sample size Bozdogan (1987)
icl -2L + q log(n) + 2 EN sample size and classification Biernacki, Celeux and Govaert (2000)
awe -2(L - EN) + 2q (1.5 + log(n)) sample size and classification Banfield and Raftery (1993)
clc -2L + 2 EN classification only Biernacki and Govaert (1997)

Lower is better for every criterion. The charge per parameter is 2 for AIC, 3 for KIC, log((n + 2) / 24) for SABIC, log(n) for BIC and log(n) + 1 for CAIC, so above a few dozen units AIC is the most lenient and CAIC the strictest of these, and a larger charge favours fewer classes. ICL and AWE add a charge for classification uncertainty, because a class that overlaps its neighbours raises EN, and so favour fewer and better separated classes than BIC. CLC has no charge per parameter, only the entropy charge, so it can favour many classes when they are well separated and few when they are not. CLC uses the entropy sum as ICL and AWE do. Some software reports a CLC built from relative entropy, which is bounded by one and charges almost nothing, and the two numbers are not comparable.

Two conventions for the sample size

In a two-level model the sample size is either the number of groups, here the 106 students, or the number of observations, the 1,422 enrolments. latents reports every criterion that depends on a sample size under both conventions: the columns ending _groups count groups and use the posterior probabilities of the group classes for EN, and the columns ending _individual count observations and use the posterior probabilities of the profiles. Neither is the definition of a multilevel BIC; they are two stated choices, and an analysis picks one and keeps it for every candidate. AIC and KIC have no sample size and carry no convention.

In a single-level grid there are no groups, the two sample sizes coincide, and BIC, SABIC and CAIC are the same under both conventions. The entropy criteria are not: their _groups columns use the classification of the group classes, of which a single-level model has one, so they carry no classification charge and ICL there equals BIC. In a single-level grid, read the _individual columns of ICL, AWE and CLC.

The table of every candidate

as.data.frame() returns one row per candidate with every criterion under both conventions, beside its log likelihood, number of parameters, classification summaries and estimation checks.

The minimum of each criterion

get_results(x, "best") reduces that table to one row per criterion and convention: the candidate at the criterion’s minimum, its numbers of classes and the minimum value. It answers “which candidate does each criterion favour?” and nothing more.

get_results(models, "best")
#>    criterion  convention         candidate n_profiles n_group_classes model value
#> 1        aic        <NA> profiles6_groups4          6               4   VVI 16703
#> 2        kic        <NA> profiles4_groups4          4               4   VVI 16769
#> 3        bic      groups profiles4_groups3          4               3   VVI 16852
#> 4        bic individuals profiles3_groups3          3               3   VVI 16973
#> 5      sabic      groups profiles6_groups4          6               4   VVI 16661
#> 6      sabic individuals profiles4_groups3          4               3   VVI 16823
#> 7       caic      groups profiles4_groups3          4               3   VVI 16903
#> 8       caic individuals profiles3_groups3          3               3   VVI 17011
#> 9        awe      groups profiles3_groups2          3               2   VVI 17169
#> 10       awe individuals profiles2_groups3          2               3   VVI 17398
#> 11       icl      groups profiles4_groups2          4               2   VVI 16881
#> 12       icl individuals profiles2_groups4          2               4   VVI 17140
#> 13       clc      groups profiles6_groups4          6               4   VVI 16580
#> 14       clc individuals profiles2_groups4          2               4   VVI 16944

Here the criteria name 8 different candidates. BIC with students as the units favours profiles4_groups3, BIC with enrolments profiles3_groups3, ICL with students profiles4_groups2, and AIC profiles6_groups4. Disagreement is the usual outcome, not a failure: the criteria were built for different purposes, and the size of their charges explains much of the disagreement: AIC, with the lightest charge, names the largest candidate, and the entropy criteria name smaller ones.

A minimum on the edge of the grid, at the largest number of profiles or group classes fitted, means the criterion was still falling there. Such a minimum says only that the range was too narrow. The range is widened until the minimum lies inside it, or, when the criterion keeps falling at every size the data can support, the size of each decrease becomes the evidence, as in the next section.

Plotting the criteria

plot() draws the criteria against the number of profiles, one line per number of group classes, and rings the lowest value of each. what names criteria by their columns, and what = "all" draws every one.

plot(models)

plot(models, what = "bic_groups")

Where added classes stop paying off

Deltas

When a criterion falls across the whole range, its minimum carries little information, but the size of each fall does. get_results(x, "deltas") reports, for every candidate, the decrease in a criterion from its neighbour with one profile fewer (delta_profile, from from_profile) and from its neighbour with one group class fewer (delta_group_class, from from_group_class). A positive delta means the added class lowered the criterion; a negative delta means it raised it. A candidate with no such neighbour in the grid has NA. The criterion is BIC with groups as the units unless using names another column.

get_results(models, "deltas")

With three group classes, the third profile lowers BIC by 85 and the fourth by 22, and the fifth raises it by 27, which the table shows as a negative decrease. The candidate with two profiles has no delta along the profiles, because its neighbour with one profile and three group classes is not identified. Shrinking falls mark the point after which further profiles add detail rather than structure, and the first negative delta marks where they stop improving the criterion at all. The deltas are plotted for both directions, along the number of profiles on the left and along the number of group classes on the right.

plot(models, what = "deltas")

Any criterion can be read this way:

plot(models, what = "deltas", using = "icl_individual")

Knees

The knee, or elbow, is where a falling curve bends from steep to flat. get_results(x, "knees") locates it by a rule inspired by Kneedle (Satopää, Albrecht, Irwin and Raghavan, 2011), simplified to its geometric core:

  1. both axes of the curve, the number of classes and the criterion, are rescaled to the unit interval;
  2. a straight line is drawn from the first candidate to the last;
  3. the knee is the candidate furthest below that line, measured perpendicular to it, and distance is that perpendicular distance in the rescaled units.

Kneedle’s smoothing and sensitivity thresholds are left out, so a nearly straight curve can still name a knee with a very small distance. The distance therefore reports the strength of the bend as well as its place. A curve whose last value is not below its first has no knee, because a bend in a rising criterion marks no diminishing return.

Knees are found along three kinds of line: along the number of profiles at each number of group classes (direction = "profiles"), along the number of group classes at each number of profiles ("group_classes"), and across all candidates ordered by their number of parameters ("parameters"). The columns from and to give the ends of the line and n_points its length.

get_results(models, "knees")
#>        direction            line  criterion              from                to n_points
#> 1       profiles   1 group class bic_groups profiles1_groups1 profiles6_groups1        6
#> 2       profiles 2 group classes bic_groups profiles2_groups2 profiles6_groups2        5
#> 3       profiles 3 group classes bic_groups profiles2_groups3 profiles6_groups3        5
#> 4       profiles 4 group classes bic_groups profiles2_groups4 profiles6_groups4        5

#> 6  group_classes      2 profiles bic_groups profiles2_groups1 profiles2_groups4        4
#> 7  group_classes      3 profiles bic_groups profiles3_groups1 profiles3_groups4        4
#> 8  group_classes      4 profiles bic_groups profiles4_groups1 profiles4_groups4        4
#> 9  group_classes      5 profiles bic_groups profiles5_groups1 profiles5_groups4        4
#> 10 group_classes      6 profiles bic_groups profiles6_groups1 profiles6_groups4        4
#> 11    parameters  all candidates bic_groups profiles1_groups1 profiles6_groups4       21
#>       knee_candidate distance knee_without_largest stable                               note
#> 1  profiles2_groups1    0.544    profiles2_groups1   TRUE                                   
#> 2  profiles4_groups2    0.648    profiles3_groups2  FALSE moves when the largest is left out
#> 3  profiles4_groups3    0.750    profiles3_groups3  FALSE moves when the largest is left out
#> 4  profiles4_groups4    0.792    profiles3_groups4  FALSE moves when the largest is left out
#> 5               <NA>       NA                 <NA>     NA        fewer than three candidates
#> 6  profiles2_groups2    0.413    profiles2_groups2   TRUE                                   
#> 7  profiles3_groups2    0.438    profiles3_groups2   TRUE                                   
#> 8  profiles4_groups2    0.439    profiles4_groups2   TRUE                                   
#> 9  profiles5_groups2    0.456    profiles5_groups2   TRUE                                   
#> 10 profiles6_groups2    0.463    profiles6_groups2   TRUE                                   
#> 11 profiles2_groups2    0.561    profiles2_groups2   TRUE

The straight line ends at the largest candidate fitted, so the knee depends on where the grid stops: fitting one more candidate moves the line and can move the knee. The table tests that directly. knee_without_largest is the knee of the same line with its last candidate removed, and stable is TRUE when the two agree. A knee that moves when the range shrinks by one candidate is weak evidence. note explains every row without a full answer:

note Meaning
empty a knee was found and is stable
fewer than three candidates a line needs three points for a knee
three candidates: stability not assessed stable needs four points
the criterion does not fall along this line no diminishing return to find
the curve does not bend below the line the curve is straight or bends upward
no knee when the largest is left out the shortened line has no knee
moves when the largest is left out the knee depends on the range fitted

With three group classes, the knee along the number of profiles is profiles4_groups3 at a distance of 0.75. Without the largest candidate it is profiles3_groups3, so stable is FALSE: the bend lies between three and four profiles, and which of the two the rule names depends on where the grid stops. The deltas locate the same region with less ambiguity, which is why the two are read together.

The criterion over the whole grid

The heatmap shows every candidate at once, coloured by how far its criterion lies above the lowest value in the grid. It reads the same criterion as the deltas and takes the same using.

plot(models, what = "heatmap")

Are the classes distinct?

A candidate can fit well and still separate its classes poorly, leaving many units between classes and their assignments uncertain. Three statistics describe the separation, each from the posterior probabilities of membership.

  • Relative entropy, 1 - EN / (n log K) for K classes, runs from 0, every unit equally likely to belong to every class, to 1, every unit certain. It summarizes a whole level in one number and is NA for a level with one class, where it is undefined rather than perfect.
  • Average posterior probability (AvePP) of a class is the mean posterior probability of that class among the units assigned to it. Values of 0.7 to 0.8 and above are commonly read as adequate separation (Nagin, 2005). It is reported per class, so a single poorly separated class is visible where entropy would average it away.
  • Odds of correct classification (OCC) of a class is (p / (1 - p)) / (r / (1 - r)), with p its AvePP and r its estimated share. It compares classification against a guess from the class size alone: near 1 is no better than the guess, and 5 or more is the usual floor for adequate separation (Nagin, 2005).

The table of candidates summarizes each level by its relative entropy and the smallest, largest and mean AvePP, and counts the classes below a cutoff of 0.8, set with cutoff. get_results(x, "classification") gives every class of every candidate: its size by modal assignment and by estimate, its AvePP, its OCC and the relative entropy of its level.

get_results(models, "classification")

plot(x, what = "diagnostics") draws relative entropy and the lowest AvePP across the candidates, with the cutoff dashed; what = "entropy" and what = "avepp" draw one of the two. For one fitted candidate, plot_diagnostics() draws the certainty of every unit in its class, the uncertainty of every unit, the class sizes and the average posterior matrix, for the profiles and, when there are two or more group classes, for the group classes (what = "group_posteriors" and the like). The two levels often differ sharply: a group is classified from all of its observations together, and an observation from its own responses alone.

plot(models, what = "diagnostics")

Classification quality is not a criterion for the number of classes in itself: a model with fewer classes is usually better separated, so choosing by entropy alone favours too few classes. It decides between candidates that the criteria leave close, and it qualifies how the chosen classes can be used, for instance whether modal assignments can stand in for the classes in a later analysis.

Can the estimate be trusted?

Estimation checks

The likelihood of a mixture model has several local maxima. A solution reached from several random starts is more credible than one reached once, and an estimate on the boundary of the parameter space, a variance at its floor or a class with almost no members, marks a model too complex for the data. plot(x, what = "trust") gives each candidate one tile, labelled with the number of starts that reached its best log likelihood, and coloured by the first problem it has:

Status Meaning
best replicated converged, inside the parameter space, best likelihood reached by more than one start
best found once as above, but only one start reached the best likelihood
on a boundary an estimate reached the edge of the parameter space
not converged the EM algorithm stopped before meeting its tolerance
not fitted (x) not identified, or failed with an error kept in the table 
plot(models, what = "trust")

A candidate found once is refitted with more starts before it is chosen. The columns converged, boundary, n_best_replicated, warnings and error of the table of candidates hold the same checks.

The smallest class

A class holding a very small share of the units is hard to interpret and estimated from little data. plot(x, what = "smallest") draws the estimated share of the smallest class of every candidate, with a dashed line at 5%, a common floor rather than a rule.

plot(models, what = "smallest")

All of the plots together

plot(x, what = "selection") returns the deltas, the heatmap, the smallest class, the estimation checks and the classification diagnostics as one list of plots, drawn in turn. using sets the criterion of the first two and cutoff the AvePP line of the last.

plot(models, what = "selection")

How the profiles divide

The tree shows how the profiles of each model divide into those of the next: each profile is linked to the profiles of the model with one more that receive its observations (Zappia and Oshlack, 2018). A profile that splits cleanly in two suggests a real distinction; one that draws from several profiles of the smaller model suggests a reshuffling.

plot(models, what = "tree")

Comparing chosen candidates

Once the evidence narrows the choice to a few candidates, compare_models() places them side by side, named or by their numbers of classes. Its table adds the difference of each candidate’s BIC from the lowest among those compared, delta_bic, and its BIC weight, exp(-delta_bic / 2) normalized over the compared candidates: the approximate posterior probability of each if one of them is true and all were equally likely beforehand (Wagenmakers and Farrell, 2004). The weights depend on which candidates are compared.

comparison <- compare_models(models, "profiles3_groups3", "profiles4_groups3",
                             "profiles4_groups2")
comparison
#> Model comparison
#> 
#> Model              Profiles  Group classes   k    LogLik       BIC   ΔBIC  Weight       ICL  Entropy  Min AvePP  < 0.8  Group entropy  Group min AvePP
#> -----------------  --------  -------------  --  --------  --------  -----  ------  --------  -------  ---------  -----  -------------  ---------------
#> profiles3_groups3         3              3  38  -8348.43  16874.07  21.92   0.000  17622.03     0.79       0.85      0           0.80             0.86
#> profiles4_groups3         4              3  51  -8307.15  16852.14   0.00   1.000  18014.13     0.74       0.80      0           0.82             0.87
#> profiles4_groups2         4              2  47  -8326.19  16871.57  19.43   0.000  18021.23     0.74       0.79      1           0.94             0.98
plot(comparison)

The model behind a row is taken out with get_candidate(), by name or by numbers of classes.

chosen <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
chosen
#> Two-level latent profile analysis: 4 profiles, 3 group classes
#> 1422 individuals in 106 groups; varying diagonal residual covariance (VVI)
#> Log likelihood: -8307.154320 | AIC: 16716.309 | BIC (groups): 16852.144
#> Converged: TRUE | iterations: 48 | best start: 3/3
#> 
#>  profile browse lectures forum_read forum_post attendance count proportion
#>        1  0.412    0.232      0.490      0.383      0.309   497      0.350
#>        2 -0.564   -0.561     -0.695     -0.676     -0.656   392      0.276
#>        3 -1.113   -0.685     -1.200     -0.880     -1.417   202      0.142
#>        4  0.728    0.734      0.821      0.763      1.180   331      0.233
#> 
#> Variances and standard errors: get_results(x, "profiles"). 
#> Every other table: get_results(x, what = ), or get_results(x, "all").

Testing one more class

The usual likelihood ratio test is invalid between mixtures with k and k + 1 classes, because the smaller model sits on the boundary of the larger one, where the statistic loses its reference distribution. bootstrap_lrt() simulates that distribution (McLachlan, 1987; Nylund, Asparouhov and Muthén, 2007): data sets are drawn from the smaller fitted model, both models are refitted to each, and the observed statistic is placed among the simulated ones. With B simulated data sets and b statistics at least as large as the observed one, the p-value is (b + 1) / (B + 1), which can never be zero and cannot fall below 1 / (B + 1). A replicate that fails a fitting check withholds the p-value rather than drop silently. The example uses 19 data sets, whose smallest attainable p-value is 0.05; applied analyses use 99 or more.

smaller <- get_candidate(models, "profiles3_groups3")
larger <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
test <- bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, data = course_engagement,
                      iter = 19, n_starts = 2, seed = 1)
test
#> Parametric bootstrap likelihood-ratio comparison
#> Null: 3 profiles, 3 group classes; alternative: 4 profiles, 3 group classes
#> Observed statistic: 82.548767
#> p-value: 0.05 (Monte Carlo SE 0.0487) from 19 of 19 valid replicates
plot(test)

Putting the evidence together

No rule turns this evidence into a number of classes, and latents does not apply one. A choice is made by reading the evidence in a fixed order and reporting every step:

  1. State the convention for the sample size before reading any criterion, and keep it.
  2. Read the minima of the criteria under that convention. Note where they agree and in which direction they disagree. A minimum on the edge of the grid calls for a wider grid.
  3. Read the deltas and knees when the criteria keep falling. Report the knee with its distance and whether it is stable.
  4. Check classification of the candidates still in contention: relative entropy, the smallest AvePP and OCC of each level.
  5. Check estimation: replication of the best likelihood, boundary estimates and the smallest class. Refit a candidate found once with more starts.
  6. Test the leading candidate against its neighbour with the bootstrap likelihood ratio test when the evidence is close.
  7. Interpret the leading candidates. Between candidates that the statistics leave close, the one whose classes are distinct and meaningful for the question is chosen, and the reason is stated.

The tables behind every step are returned by the verbs above, so the reported choice can be reproduced from the reported evidence.

Functions

Call Result
as.data.frame(models) One row per candidate: every criterion, classification summaries and checks
get_results(models, “best”) The candidate at the minimum of each criterion and convention
plot(models), plot(models, what = “bic_groups”), what = “all” Criteria across the candidates, lowest ringed
get_results(models, “deltas”, using = ) Decrease in a criterion from one profile fewer and one group class fewer
plot(models, what = “deltas”, using = ) The decreases along profiles and along group classes
get_results(models, “knees”, using = ) Chord-distance knee of each line, with its stability
plot(models, what = “heatmap”, using = ) Distance of every candidate from the lowest criterion
get_results(models, “classification”) Size, AvePP, OCC and entropy of every class of every candidate
get_results(models, “candidates”, cutoff = ) The table of candidates with another AvePP cutoff
plot(models, what = “diagnostics”, “entropy” or “avepp”, cutoff = ) Relative entropy and lowest AvePP across the candidates
plot(models, what = “trust”) Convergence, boundary and replication of every candidate
plot(models, what = “smallest”) Share of the smallest class of every candidate
plot(models, what = “selection”) Deltas, heatmap, smallest class, trust and diagnostics together
plot(models, what = “tree”) How the profiles divide as more are added
compare_models(models, “name”, …) Chosen candidates side by side, with BIC weights
get_candidate(models, “name”) One fitted candidate
bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, data, iter) Bootstrap likelihood ratio test of k against k + 1 classes
